# How to become a trusted third-party safety evaluator (synthesis)

Fetched/compiled: 2026-10-19. This synthesises the evaluator files in this directory, the lab-side statements in `lab-statements-on-third-party-testing.md`, and the 2026 policy instruments. Every criterion below cites where a lab or an evaluator stated or demonstrated it. Claims not traceable to a fetched document are marked UNVERIFIED.

## 0. What "trusted" currently buys (the access ladder, as of October 2026)
Observed access tiers, from least to most, with documented examples:
1. **Public models only, no lab relationship**: Palisade (shutdown resistance, chess hacking, self-replication), Nightingale Collective (OSINT on agent incidents), Holistic AI, Enkrypt, Promptfoo, MLCommons AILuminate, FLI AI Safety Index, SaferAI. Influence comes from reproducibility and public attention, not access.
2. **Paid red-team / benchmark vendor with pre-release checkpoints**: Gray Swan (OpenAI o1, GPT-5; Anthropic Sonnet 4.5 to Opus 5; Google Gemini 3.7/4; named in system cards), Irregular (cyber assessments for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta since Feb 2025), Scale (US AISI-authorised evaluator, Feb 2025; no system-card naming verified), Faculty (OpenAI red teaming, per Altman quote on faculty.ai).
3. **Independent nonprofit assessor with helpful-only models, early checkpoints, chain-of-thought and zero-data-retention endpoints**: METR (OpenAI o1 to GPT-5.6 Sol; Anthropic Claude 3.7 to Opus 5.5), Apollo Research (OpenAI o1 to GPT-6 Astra; three days on Astra with two days of CoT access), SecureBio (GPT-5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra "bio-railfree" checkpoints; Anthropic risk-report chapters). OpenAI's description: "secure access to early model checkpoints, select evaluation results ..., zero-data retention where needed, and models with fewer mitigations", and "direct chain-of-thought access" for several organisations (OpenAI 2025-11-19).
4. **Government institutes**: UK AISI and US CAISI (pre-deployment testing of OpenAI, Anthropic, and from May 2026 Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI in CAISI's pre-deployment review program; see `uk-aisi.md`, `us-caisi.md`). UK AISI reports in the GPT-6 Astra card include a cyber test where "internet access appears incidentally enabled".
5. **Methodology / document review with unredacted internal material**: METR's review of OpenAI's gpt-oss adversarial fine-tuning (NDA; OpenAI approval of the post; 17 recommendations, 9 adopted) and of Anthropic's unredacted Sabotage Risk Reports (Opus 4/4.1, Opus 4.6); SecureBio's review of the chem/bio chapter of Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report.
6. **Entity-level / embedded access**: METR Frontier Risk Report (Feb-Mar 2026: internal SOTA models of Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI incl. raw CoT); METR/Redwood six days on OpenAI premises for the Hugging Face incident with ~1,300 raw-CoT transcripts and nine interviews; Anthropic "Tier 3": six METR staff with badges, hardware and internal tools "roughly on par" with internal risk-assessment teams, publication without veto (2026-10-15); Accenture/Faculty "access comparable to an employee's" with $1B each over five years (2026-09-18).

No arrangement in the record gives an external evaluator power to delay a release (secondary census at digitalapplied.com, 2026-10-16, UNVERIFIED beyond that source; consistent with every primary document fetched).

## 1. Criteria the labs state explicitly
| Criterion | Anthropic (2026-10-15; Amodei Sept 2026) | OpenAI (2025-11-19; 2026-09-22) | Frontier Model Forum (2025-08-04) | Law/policy (2026) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expertise | one of four requirements | "demonstrate relevant technical expertise"; incident work needs "cyber forensics expertise, alignment expertise, large-scale chain of thought analysis" | replication needs "technical proficiency in AI architectures with domain expertise"; open-ended work needs "strong capability elicitation skills" | CA SB 813 IVOs must show "expertise in AI risk assessment, including the metrics and methodologies" |
| Independence | "shouldn't hold equity in the company" and not "financially or operationally dependent on it" | "identify, disclose, and address organizational and individual conflicts of interest, including financial incentives, relationships with developers, and prior involvement"; "recusal or appropriate exclusion periods"; "No payment is ever contingent on the results" | replication assessors "must maintain independence from the development process" | AB 1405: no audit where an interest "would reasonably be expected to impair objectivity"; no auditing own work; 12-month cooling-off for staff with material responsibility at the auditee |
| Sufficient access | tiers 1-3; employee-like for Tier 3 | "Proportionate access ... within the bounds of legal, security, and IP constraints"; helpful-only models and CoT "where necessary" | confirmation may need model access to replicate; adversarial testing needs representative safeguards | White House Accord: "independent external auditor or evaluator" assesses whether controls "are operating as intended" |
| Security | small team under "enforceable agreements", other staff siloed, works under Anthropic security standards; architecture info needs explicit approval | "information-security practices and enforceable confidentiality protections covering their personnel"; else "company-managed devices or premises" | "strict data handling protocols, maintain confidentiality agreements", demonstrate capacity before privileged access; minimum-necessary information | - |
| Methodological rigour | - | "pre-registered" claims; "distinguish direct findings from interpretation, explain uncertainty"; justify criteria where no standard exists | "clear documentation of evaluation approaches, comprehensive results reporting", "transparency about limitations and uncertainties" | AB 1405 reports must include scope, results, remediation, limitations, signed statement; 10-year record retention |
| Freedom to publish | no veto; redaction only of predefined categories; evaluator may say whether redactions were justified | assessors "maintain editorial independence"; labs may request redactions and get "a reasonable period to remediate"; (2025 contracts: publication "submitted to OpenAI for review and approval") | protocols for sharing findings still "under development" | - |

## 1b. The evaluators' own standard: AEF-1 (AI Evaluator Forum, v1, 2025-12-04)
Written by METR, Transluce, SecureBio, AVERI, Epoch, Princeton, Stanford, GovAI, CIP, Meridian Labs and Oxford authors (`ai-evaluator-forum.md`), AEF-1 is a publishable checklist with five principles: Sufficient Access and Resources (black-box API at minimum; safeguard-minimised versions for worst-case misuse; reasoning traces/activations where relevant; "at least 20 business days" for novel systems; legal safe harbor), Minimized Conflicts of Interest (no results-contingent pay; no provider equity or board seats; published COI policy; disclosure of payments, funding share, equity and dual roles; recusal for direct equity), Analytic Autonomy (evaluator controls metrics, elicitation, scaffolding, rubrics; editorial control over presentation incl. scope and access limits), Transparent Methods and Results (methodology sufficient for review; representative examples released; provider "did not have authority to redact results to conceal concerning findings"; redaction disclaimer), and Protection of Sensitive Information (permission before publishing on non-public systems; provider may not train on or retain held-out eval data; evaluator security controls; responsible-disclosure policy). METR (Frontier Risk Report), Transluce (mental-health evaluation) and SecureBio (GPT-6 Astra assessment) have attached the checklist to reports; the EU AI Office reportedly endorsed key provisions for GPAI Code of Practice compliance (UNVERIFIED from primary). Apollo's published norms (fair-market compensation never contingent on outcome; model-identity-hiding internal APIs; air-gapped data rooms for white-box access) and UK AISI's position that third parties gain "legitimacy through their independence and absence of conflicts of interest" while "the science is too nascent for independent evaluations to act as a 'certification' function" (Oct 2024) point the same way.

## 2. What the trusted evaluators actually did (demonstrated criteria)
### 2.1 Methodological rigour and public method
- METR: open task standard and Vivaria; time-horizon methodology paper with bootstrap CIs; rescoring reward hacks as failures (o3 1-2%; GPT-5 18/789 runs); capability-elicitation guidelines with a "safety margin" for post-training enhancements; "Notes on" limitations in every report (`metr.md`).
- Apollo: "We need a science of evals" position; scheming evals reported with per-environment rates and explicit caveats that "low rates of misbehavior here do not provide substantial evidence about the model's alignment or misalignment" given eval awareness (GPT-6 Astra card sec. 8.8.1; `apollo-research.md`).
- SecureBio: expert baselines built into VCT (22.1% expert accuracy, 36 experts per the Astra card's citation); refusal-corrected accuracy; holdout sets with canaries; summary statistics only so developers cannot optimise per task (`securebio.md`).
- Irregular: public difficulty framework (SOLVE), cost-per-success metric, pre-run difficulty prediction and dated snapshots in FrontierCyber (`irregular.md`).
- Gray Swan: public dated leaderboards with raw counts, k=1/10/100 attack-success curves, UK AISI/CAISI co-judging and appeals (`gray-swan.md`).
- UK AISI: Inspect as the shared open framework (Anthropic's 2024 eval initiative asks for "the Inspect or METR standard"); documented limitations in each system-card section ("tested a small band of undesired behaviors") (`uk-aisi.md`).

### 2.2 Reproducibility and open tooling
Evaluators that received deep access had first released tooling others could run: METR (Vivaria, task-standard, eval-analysis-public), UK AISI (inspect_ai, inspect_evals, ControlArena), Gray Swan (ART/IPI benchmarks and papers), Palisade (all code public), Transluce (Docent), Redwood (control code), SecureBio (WMDP; VCT gated by export control), Irregular (SOLVE spec only). The FMF notes replication "demands substantial time and computational resources", which is why labs value evaluators with their own infrastructure (OpenAI chose a methodology review for gpt-oss because worst-case fine-tuning "requires infrastructure and technical expertise that is not commonly available outside of major AI labs").

### 2.3 Novel, decision-relevant findings
Access followed findings that labs could not produce or would not have surfaced themselves: Apollo's in-context scheming (Dec 2024) led to Apollo sections in every OpenAI reasoning-model card; METR's time horizon became OpenAI's cited external benchmark; Gray Swan's "every model broken on every behaviour" arena result (62k breaks, 22 models) preceded its naming in Anthropic and Google cards; Irregular's zero-day discoveries during assessments; SecureBio's VCT showing o3 at the 94th expert percentile; Palisade's shutdown-resistance numbers (o3 79/100) with no access at all. OpenAI's own framing: third parties should "challenge our assumptions, identify risks we may have missed" (2026-09-22).

### 2.4 Responsible disclosure
- Vulnerabilities: Irregular withholds exploit details "because some vulnerabilities may still be present in deployed systems" and runs responsible disclosure with vendors; OpenAI withheld product names in the Astra card.
- Infohazards: SecureBio redacts or withholds infohazardous material but states whether the redaction affects conclusions; VCT is export-controlled and gated to organisations "with a track record in biosecurity and/or AI safety".
- Lab confidentiality: METR uses animal codenames and six confidentiality levels; Anthropic's categories (customer data, privileged material, architecture) and OpenAI's "Non-Public Models" outputs are the standard redaction classes.
- Incidents: METR/Redwood published a redaction summary and negotiated wording; Nightingale published without documented pre-notification (a contrast the labs' principles do not address).

### 2.5 Security of model access
- METR: SOC 2 Type I, FIDO2-only identity, per-evaluation secret repo forks, public disclosure of its own 2026 security incidents (`metr.md`). SecureBio: ISO/IEC 27001:2022. Gray Swan: SOC 2, Cyber Essentials. Anthropic requires Tier-3 staff to work "under Anthropic's security standards"; OpenAI will move insufficiently secure assessors onto "company-managed devices or premises". The FMF makes demonstrated security a precondition for privileged access.
- The cost of failure is visible: OpenAI fired three safety researchers in October 2026 for sharing "sensitive information" with an outside group (SF Standard 2026-10-17), and Anthropic names evaluators' work with other companies as a leak risk.

### 2.6 Publishing norms and "process transparency"
- Every METR report carries a "Note on independence" stating NDA terms, payment (usually none), and whether the lab had approval rights (GPT-5: "OpenAI's comms and legal team required review and approval of this post"); METR's COI policy calls this "process transparency": readers are told "what access we had and what information was redacted", or that there were undisclosed redactions.
- SecureBio: "AI developers have no authority to redact our results to conceal performance or unfavorable findings"; publishes errata.
- FAR.AI: retains publication rights for non-confidential insights, "declined contracts that restricted this", will not accept terms preventing comment on public models, labels research informed by paid work.
- OpenAI's 2025 contract excerpts and METR's gpt-oss review show the baseline many evaluators accept: lab review for confidentiality and accuracy before publication; OpenAI's 2026 principles move to editorial independence plus redaction requests and a remediation window.

### 2.7 Independence and funding structure
- METR: no funding from AI companies or their employees; no equity; employees of frontier companies ineligible for the board; recusal tiers for employment, equity, relationships, gifts over $100; disclosure in reports when proceeding with a conflict (COI policy v1.1, effective 2026-10-09).
- FAR.AI: for-profit developer consulting capped at 10% of revenue, share disclosed.
- SecureBio: never result-contingent funding; discloses funding in every report; public FCOI policy.
- Counter-examples the field debates: Gray Swan (labs are paying customers; founder on OpenAI's board with recusal), Accenture/Faculty (funded directly by Anthropic), Scale (commercial data vendor to labs), Epoch's FrontierMath (OpenAI funding and ownership of tiers, disclosed late). The ICML 2026 mapping found 68% of 519 evaluations in 75 system cards were internal and that some third parties are "funded by the developers they evaluate".

## 3. Checklist for a new third-party safety lab (derived)
1. **Pick a narrow, consequential question** that matches a lab's framework category (CBRN, cyber, autonomy/AI R&D, scheming/sabotage, safeguards robustness, monitorability, incident investigation). OpenAI's four 2026 priority areas and Anthropic's 2024 eval wish-list are explicit demand signals.
2. **Build and open-source the harness first**, ideally on Inspect or the METR task standard; publish with bootstrap CIs, expert baselines, held-out splits with canaries, and a limitations section. Show results on public models before asking for private ones (Apollo, Palisade, Gray Swan, Irregular all did).
3. **Produce one finding the lab did not have**, and report it in the lab's own vocabulary (thresholds, k-attempt ASR, time horizon, refusal-corrected accuracy).
4. **Adopt a written COI and funding policy** (no result-contingent pay; disclose developer revenue; recusal rules; board independence) and publish it before the first engagement; METR's, Transluce's and FAR.AI's are the templates; attach the AEF-1 checklist to every report; California AB 1405/SB 813 will make parts of this statutory for registered auditors by 2028-2029; apply to the AI Evaluator Forum once you "conduct and publish rigorous independent technical evaluations".
5. **Get security certified and prove operational discipline**: SOC 2 / ISO 27001, hardware keys, per-engagement compartments, a published incident-disclosure norm. Expect to work on lab hardware or premises until then.
6. **Negotiate publication terms in writing and disclose them**: what access you had, who could review, what was redacted; keep the right to say a redaction was material. Accept remediation windows for vulnerabilities and infohazards.
7. **Handle hazards responsibly**: coordinated disclosure for zero-days; gate or export-control CBRN items; summary-level reporting on held-out tasks.
8. **Say what you could not conclude.** The most-cited evaluators are those that caveat hardest (Apollo on eval awareness; METR on cheating-inflated horizons; AISI on "small band of undesired behaviors").
9. **Staff with people who have operated inside labs but are not currently paid by them**, and disclose that history (SF Standard 2026-10-17; Palisade/METR founders).
10. **Plan for launch-agnostic, entity-level work** (internal deployments, training-time alignment, incident response), which is where both OpenAI and Anthropic say the next access will go, and which requires forensic and large-scale CoT-analysis capacity (OpenAI 2026-09-22; METR Frontier Risk Report).

## 4. Open problems the record does not resolve
- No shared accreditation standard exists (FMF 2025; Anthropic 2026-09-18 "no standards yet exist"); California's IVO criteria arrive 2027-2028.
- Time budgets are short (Apollo three days on Astra; METR/Redwood six days on-site) and no evaluator can delay a release.
- Funding: labs want pooled or government funding (Anthropic), OpenAI pays and says payment is never result-contingent, METR refuses lab money; the field has not converged.
- Undisclosed incidents found by outsiders (Nightingale) show that embedded access does not substitute for external monitoring.
